## 1. What you'll build, and why

This is the last hop, and the payoff. You'll write **IRGen** — lower the SIL module to **LLVM IR** —
and `clang` turns that into a native executable. Phase 1 already ran programs, but only
straight-line ones: `let`, `var`, arithmetic and `print`, top to bottom. Concepts 05–08 added
types, control flow and functions without running any of it. Here they run for the first time —
`if`/`while`/`for`, functions and recursion execute, and `swiftml2`'s output matches `swiftc`
byte-for-byte. That's **Milestone M2**, and the end of Phase 2.

@fig-pipeline puts this hop in place. Every stage to its left is already written: the lexer (01),
the parser (02), the type checker (03, 05–07) and SILGen (08). IRGen is the arrow from SIL to LLVM
IR, and after it `clang` compiles and links, so `./a.out` runs.

![The complete Phase-2 pipeline: source → tokens → AST → typed AST → SIL → LLVM IR → native. IRGen (concept 09) is the last hop; then `clang` links it and the program runs.](figs/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline}

- **You implement:** the lowering in `irgen.ml` — the instruction each operator becomes
  (`binop_instruction`), the entry-block allocas (`gen_allocas`), the other instructions
  (`gen_instr`) and the terminators (`gen_term`). Everything upstream (front-end, SIL, SILGen) is given and complete.
- **Outcome:** `swiftml2 build foo.swift -o foo && ./foo` produces the same output as `swiftc`.

Here is a complete example to keep in view while you fill the skeleton. It has one function with
parameters of two different types, then calls that function from the top level:

```swift
func choose(_ value: Int, _ addOne: Bool) -> Int {
  if addOne {
    return value + 1
  }
  return value
}

print(choose(41, true))
```

Concept 08's SILGen has already turned it into this SIL — the **input** to the IRGen you write here:

```
sil @choose(%0 : $Int, %1 : $Bool) -> $Int {
bb0:
  %2 = alloc_stack $Int  // value
  store %0 to %2
  %4 = alloc_stack $Bool  // addOne
  store %1 to %4
  %6 = load %4 $Bool
  cond_br %6, bb1, bb2
bb1:
  %7 = load %2 $Int
  %8 = integer_literal $Int, 1
  %9 = binop "+" %7, %8 $Int
  return %9
bb2:
  %10 = load %2 $Int
  return %10
}

sil @main() -> $() {
bb0:
  %0 = integer_literal $Int, 41
  %1 = integer_literal $Bool, true
  %2 = function_ref @choose
  %3 = apply %2(%0, %1)
  %4 = apply @print(%3)
  return
}
```

and `swiftml2 --emit-llvm` turns that into this unoptimized LLVM module:

```llvm
; swiftml Phase-2 LLVM IR
declare i32 @printf(ptr, ...)
@.fmt_int = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c"%lld\0A\00"
@.fmt_str = private unnamed_addr constant [4 x i8] c"%s\0A\00"
@.fmt_dbl = private unnamed_addr constant [4 x i8] c"%g\0A\00"
@.btrue  = private unnamed_addr constant [5 x i8] c"true\00"
@.bfalse = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c"false\00"

define i64 @choose(i64 %arg0, i1 %arg1) {
bb0:
  %t0 = alloca i64
  %t1 = alloca i1
  store i64 %arg0, ptr %t0
  store i1 %arg1, ptr %t1
  %t2 = load i1, ptr %t1
  br i1 %t2, label %bb1, label %bb2
bb1:
  %t3 = load i64, ptr %t0
  %t4 = add i64 %t3, 1
  ret i64 %t4
bb2:
  %t5 = load i64, ptr %t0
  ret i64 %t5
}

define i32 @main() {
bb0:
  %t0 = call i64 @choose(i64 41, i1 1)
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t0)
  ret i32 0
}

```

Read the two side by side and the mapping is almost line for line: the same blocks with the same
names, `alloc_stack` → `alloca`, `load` → `load`, `cond_br` → `br i1`, `return %9` → `ret i64`. The
exceptions are the ones to watch in `gen_instr`. Literals and `function_ref` produce **no** LLVM
line: `integer_literal $Int, 1` just becomes the operand `1` in `add i64 %t3, 1`, and `@choose`
appears directly in the `call`. The value numbers change too — SIL's `%9` is LLVM's `%t4` — which is
what the operand table is for. And `@main` returns `i32 0` to the operating system rather than
nothing.

The declarations and format strings are given scaffolding. A format string is an LLVM byte
array: `c"…"` writes the bytes as text, and `\XX` is one byte in hexadecimal — `\0A` the newline,
`\00` the zero byte that ends every C string. So `c"%lld\0A\00"` is the six bytes `%`, `l`, `l`,
`d`, newline, zero, which is why its type is `[6 x i8]`. `private` keeps the global inside this
module, `unnamed_addr` says its address does not matter (LLVM may merge identical strings), and
`constant` makes it read-only.

`Int` becomes `i64`, while `Bool`
becomes `i1`, a one-bit integer. `@choose` receives `%arg0` and `%arg1`, stores them in the stack
slots used by raw SIL, and branches on the loaded `Bool`. Each branch returns an `i64`.

In `@main`, the literals `41` and `true` appear directly as the operands `41` and `1`. The call
produces `%t0`, which the `printf` call consumes. Temporary numbering restarts in each function,
which is why both functions can have a `%t0`. The final `ret i32 0` reports successful process
termination. Compiling and running the module prints `42`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### The easy hop — because SIL did the hard work

IRGen is the shortest pass in the compiler, and that's the point: **SILGen already built the
control-flow graph, so IRGen is almost a one-to-one transliteration.** SIL is raw and memory-based;
LLVM IR is also memory-capable (it has `alloca`/`load`/`store`) and block-structured.

This concept adds no Swift syntax — the grammar is still concept 07's. What it adds is the mapping
between two IRs, so this table is the specification of your work: every SIL form concept 08 can
emit, and the LLVM line it becomes, with who writes it — you, in the four `TODO(09)` holes, or
the given code around them.

**Instructions** (`gen_instr`). Most SIL instructions become one LLVM line, but a few become
**no line at all**. Take `%8 = integer_literal $Int, 1` from the example above. LLVM has no
instruction that just produces a constant — a constant is written directly where it is used. So
IRGen emits nothing for `%8`; it only records that `%8` is spelled `1`, and when the `binop` that
uses `%8` is lowered, it looks that up and writes `add i64 %t3, 1`. That recording is
`bind_operand`, and it is all that the literals and `function_ref` do — the rows below that say
"no line".

In the table, `$T` stands for a SIL type. `<ty>`, `<ty-a>`, `<ty-b>`, and `<ret>` stand for the
corresponding LLVM type spellings produced by `llvm_type`, such as `i64`, `i1`, `double`, or `void`.

| SIL | LLVM | written by |
|---|---|---|
| `%n = integer_literal $Int, 7` | no line: wherever `%n` is used, `7` is written instead | given |
| `%n = integer_literal $Bool, true` | no line: `1` is written instead | given |
| `%n = float_literal $Double, 1.5` | no line: a hex float is written instead | given |
| `%n = string_literal $String, "hi"` | a `private unnamed_addr constant` global | given |
| `%n = alloc_stack $T  // x` | `%tK = alloca <ty>`, hoisted to the entry block | you, in `gen_allocas` |
| `%n = load %a $T` | `%tK = load <ty>, ptr %a` | you |
| `store %v to %a` | `store <ty> %v, ptr %a` — no result | you |
| `%n = binop "+" %a, %b $Int` | `%tK = add i64 %a, %b` — the instruction picked from the operator and the type | you, in `binop_instruction` |
| `%n = unop "-" %a $T` | `%tK = sub i64 0, %a` for `Int`; `%tK = fneg double %a` for `Double` | you |
| `%n = function_ref @f` | no line: `@f` is written instead | you |
| `%n = apply %f(%a, %b)` | `%tK = call <ret> %f(<ty-a> %a, <ty-b> %b)`, or `call void …` with no result | you |
| `%n = apply @print(%a)` | a `printf` call — by calling the given `gen_print` | you |

The three literal rows are already written in the skeleton, and `function_ref` is the same shape:
copy how the `Int` literal case uses `bind_operand`.

**Terminators** (`gen_term`) — the CFG. All of them are yours, and all but one map straight
across:

| SIL | LLVM |
|---|---|
| `br bbN` | `br label %bbN` |
| `cond_br %c, bbT, bbF` | `br i1 %c, label %bbT, label %bbF` |
| `return %v` | `ret <the function's return type> %v` |
| `return` | `ret void` — **but `ret i32 0` in `@main`** |
| `unreachable` | `unreachable` — a real LLVM instruction |

The exception is `@main`. In SIL it is an ordinary function returning `$()`; in LLVM it is the C
entry point, whose `i32` result *is* the process's exit code, so a valueless `return` there has to
become `ret i32 0`. Blocks and their labels carry across unchanged, which is why an `--emit-llvm`
dump closely follows the structure of the `--emit-sil` dump for the same program, even though the
instructions use LLVM syntax.

**Every `alloca` in the entry block.** One LLVM rule is worth learning right now, and
`gen_allocas` is where you apply it. An `alloca` reserves stack space that is only returned when
the *function exits* — not at the end of a scope. Here is a `let` inside a loop, and where SILGen
puts its slot:

```swift
var i = 0
while i < 3 {
  let d = i * 2
  print(d)
  i = i + 1
}
```

```
bb0:
  %1 = alloc_stack $Int  // i
  ...
bb2:                     // the loop body
  %8 = binop "*" %6, %7 $Int
  %9 = alloc_stack $Int  // d
  store %8 to %9
  ...
  br bb1
```

Lowered where it stands, `%9` would become an `alloca` in `bb2` and take a fresh slot on every
trip round the loop. Three trips are harmless; three million need at least 24 MB, and the stack is
8 MB (`run-control.t` runs exactly that loop). So `gen_allocas` runs once, at the top of `bb0`,
and emits the `alloca` for every `alloc_stack` in the function, from every block; the
`alloc_stack` case of `gen_instr` then emits nothing. Here is the whole function IRGen writes for
the loop:

```llvm
define i32 @main() {
bb0:
  %t0 = alloca i64                 ; i   <- written by gen_allocas
  %t1 = alloca i64                 ; d   <- written by gen_allocas, moved up from bb2
  store i64 0, ptr %t0
  br label %bb1
bb1:
  %t2 = load i64, ptr %t0
  %t3 = icmp slt i64 %t2, 3
  br i1 %t3, label %bb2, label %bb3
bb2:
  %t4 = load i64, ptr %t0
  %t5 = mul i64 %t4, 2
  store i64 %t5, ptr %t1           ; SIL: store %8 to %9
  %t6 = load i64, ptr %t1
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t6)
  %t7 = load i64, ptr %t0
  %t8 = add i64 %t7, 1
  store i64 %t8, ptr %t0
  br label %bb1
bb3:
  ret i32 0
}
```

The stack frame is now fixed-size: two slots, whatever the number of trips.

Moving `d`'s `alloca` up does not break anything that refers to it. The `%tN` names are handed out
in the order the lines are *written*, and `gen_allocas` writes first, so the slots get `%t0` and
`%t1` and the numbering simply carries on from `%t2`. And the store in `bb2` does not find its slot
by position: IRGen's table (`bind_operand`) says SIL `%9` is LLVM `%t1`, so `store %8 to %9`
becomes `store i64 %t5, ptr %t1` no matter which block the `alloca` sits in.

Entry-block allocation is also what LLVM's own `mem2reg` pass requires before it will promote a
slot to a register.

The control-flow work — turning a tree into a graph and threading `break`/`continue` to the right
blocks — happened in SILGen. IRGen walks that finished graph and translates it to LLVM. This
separation is one reason for having SIL. SIL also gives later compiler passes a stable, Swift-aware
representation to verify, analyze, and optimize before lowering it to a backend.

### The one real job: a value map, and *types*

IRGen maintains one table. It maps each **SIL value `%n` to an LLVM operand**. A constant maps to
itself (`Int_lit 5` becomes the operand `5`); a `string_literal` maps to a global; every other
instruction emits an LLVM line and maps the SIL value to a fresh `%tK`. The subtle part is
**types**. LLVM is strongly typed and each instruction names its operand type, so an `add` on `Int`
is `add i64` but on `Double` is `fadd double`; a comparison is `icmp` on integers and `fcmp` on
floats, and either one produces an `i1`, LLVM's Bool. Two more choices hide in that table:

- **Signed or unsigned.** An LLVM `i64` has no sign — it is 64 bits — so the sign lives in the
  instruction instead: `sdiv` or `udiv`, `srem` or `urem`, `icmp slt` or `icmp ult`. Swift's `Int`
  is signed, so it is always the `s` form. `udiv` would read `-7` as 18446744073709551609, and
  `icmp ult` would say `-1 < 0` is false.
- **Ordered or unordered.** A floating-point comparison is *ordered* (`fcmp olt`: false if either
  side is NaN) or *unordered* (`fcmp ult`: true if either side is NaN). Which one a language wants
  is not Swift's choice: the floating-point standard, IEEE 754, fixes it, and Swift, C and Java
  all follow it. A NaN is "not a number" — the result of `0.0 / 0.0` — so it is not less than,
  greater than, or equal to anything, itself included: `==`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` are all false
  on a NaN, the ordered forms. `!=` is defined as "not `==`", so it is TRUE on a NaN: `fcmp une`,
  "unordered or not equal". That is why `x != x` is true exactly when `x` is a NaN.

The SIL function's `val_ty` map gives you each value's type, and `binop_instruction` picks the
instruction from it (§3).

`print` lowers to a `printf` call keyed on the argument's type: `%lld` for `Int`, a `select` between
`"true"`/`"false"` globals for `Bool`, `%s` for a `String`. And `@main` returns `i32` (the C entry
point: `return` → `ret i32 0`), while other functions return their declared LLVM type.

### Running checks what structure alone cannot

Concept 08 could *emit* SIL but not run it. Concept 09 adds Phase 2's end-to-end semantic check.
Consider a plausible IRGen mistake: lowering SIL `sub %a, %b` as LLVM `sub i64 %b, %a`. The LLVM is
well formed, and a structural test that only looks for `sub i64` passes, but `print(9 - 4)` prints
`-5` instead of `5`. Building and running the program exposes the reversed operands.

This is the lesson behind the whole project's testing strategy: structural checks catch mistakes in
the IR's shape, while **behavioral parity against `swiftc`** catches well-formed IR with the wrong
meaning. That is why the cram tests here inspect the LLVM and also **build and run the programs**.

### Handing off to LLVM (and what we're not doing yet)

We emit *unoptimized* LLVM IR and let `clang` assemble and link it. `clang` runs LLVM's own optimizer
and backend — so even our naive, load/store-heavy IR comes out as decent native code. swiftc does the
same handoff, but only after its **own** SIL optimizer runs first (that's Phase 4 for us). Two things
we deliberately scope out, all documented:

- **`Double` printing** isn't matched to swiftc. Swift prints just enough decimal digits to
  preserve the exact `Double` value when the text is parsed again; C's `%g` does not.
  **`String`** concatenation and comparison need a runtime we haven't built. The parity corpus
  therefore covers `Int`, `Bool`, control flow, functions, and `Double` computations whose result
  is observed through a `Bool`.
- **Definite initialization** — Swift's mandatory "variable used before being initialized" pass on
  the SIL CFG — is *vacuous* for us, because every `let`/`var` is initialized at its declaration.
  Adding uninitialized `var x: Int` and a definite-initialization dataflow pass (Exercise 1) is
  the genuine version, and a direct sequel to the "missing return" analysis from concept 07.

> Oracle: `swift/lib/IRGen/IRGenSIL.cpp` is `visitSILInstruction` for each SIL opcode — the analogue
> of your `gen_instr`. swiftc's IRGen is far larger because it also lowers ARC, generics, and value
> witnesses; ours handles the Phase-2 subset.

### The diagnostics you emit

**None, again.** IRGen runs on SIL that sema accepted and the verifier passed, so there is nothing
left for it to refuse: every wording the tests compare belongs to concepts 05–07, and `--emit-llvm`
and `build` run the whole front end first and bail on its errors before IRGen is reached.

Two failures are still possible, and neither is a Swift diagnostic. Ill-typed LLVM — an `add i64` on
an `i1`, a `ret void` where the signature says `i64` — is caught by **clang**, which prints its own
error and makes `build` fail; treat that as a bug in your mapping table, and note that it is a real
check the cram files lean on (`irgen-terms.t` ends by building the program, not just printing it).
Second, the exit code: `@main`'s `ret i32 0` is the *process's* exit status, so a program that
prints nothing must still exit 0 — `run-arith.t` pins that, because it is the kind of thing that
only shows up when something later depends on it.

## 3. Build it, step by step

One skeleton, `irgen.ml`, with four holes:

- **`binop_instruction`** — which LLVM instruction each operator becomes, for each operand type.
  It is a plain function at the top of the file, a lookup table with no LLVM to emit;
- **`gen_allocas`** — one `alloca` for every stack slot of the function;
- **`gen_instr`** — the other SIL instructions: `load`, `store`, `unop`, `function_ref`,
  `apply` and `print`. It is called once per instruction, so it is a `match` with a case for
  each;
- **`gen_term`** — the four terminators, `br`, `cond_br`, `return` and `unreachable`, again one
  case each.

Everything around them is given:

| given | what it does |
|---|---|
| `emit "…"` | append a line of LLVM IR to the function |
| `fresh_temp ()` | a new LLVM register name, `%t0`, `%t1`, … |
| `bind_operand value op` / `lookup_operand value` | record / read the LLVM operand that stands for a SIL value |
| `value_type value`, `llvm_type ty` | a SIL value's type, and its LLVM spelling (`i64`, `double`, `i1`, `ptr`, `void`) |
| `gen_binop` | the whole `binop` line around your `binop_instruction`: the zero guard on `Int` `/` and `%`, the operands, the result's binding |
| `gen_print value` | the whole `print`, per type |

Do them in this order; each has a lab mode that stops before the next one is reached.

**1. The binop table, `binop_instruction`.** It returns one string: the instruction and its
operand type, such as `"add i64"` or `"fcmp olt double"`. The given `gen_binop` writes the rest
of the line around it. Choose it from `operator` (an `Ast.binop`: `Add`, `Sub`, …, `Eq`, `Lt`,
…) and `operand_type`, which is the OPERANDS' type: a comparison's own result is a `Bool` (the
SIL prints `binop "<" %3, %4 $Bool`), but `1 < 2` still needs `icmp slt i64`. Every pair that arrives, and
the string it needs (a dash: that operator does not exist at that type):

| Swift | `Ast.binop` | `Int` | `Double` | `Bool` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | `Add` | `add i64` | `fadd double` | — |
| `-` | `Sub` | `sub i64` | `fsub double` | — |
| `*` | `Mul` | `mul i64` | `fmul double` | — |
| `/` | `Div` | `sdiv i64` | `fdiv double` | — |
| `%` | `Mod` | `srem i64` | — | — |
| `==` | `Eq` | `icmp eq i64` | `fcmp oeq double` | `icmp eq i1` |
| `!=` | `Ne` | `icmp ne i64` | `fcmp une double` | `icmp ne i1` |
| `<` | `Lt` | `icmp slt i64` | `fcmp olt double` | — |
| `<=` | `Le` | `icmp sle i64` | `fcmp ole double` | — |
| `>` | `Gt` | `icmp sgt i64` | `fcmp ogt double` | — |
| `>=` | `Ge` | `icmp sge i64` | `fcmp oge double` | — |

The `s` in `sdiv`, `srem` and `slt` is signed, and the `o`/`u` in `fcmp` ordered/unordered; §2
says why each is the right one. Nothing else reaches `gen_binop`: `&&` and `||` became branches
in SILGen (08), and `String` operators are not lowered in this subset, so a catch-all `failwith`
is the right last case. `irgen-binop.t` reads `--binop-table <type>`, which calls your function
for every operator of that type and prints the answers: no program is compiled, so it goes green
before any other hole is written.

**2. `gen_allocas`.** Every function calls it at the top of its entry block, so nothing that
compiles a program runs until it exists. For every `alloc_stack` in the function — in every block,
not only `bb0` — emit `%tK = alloca <ty>` with a `fresh_temp ()`, and `bind_operand` the SIL value
to it, so the `load`s and `store`s that name the slot find it. Walk the blocks and their
instructions in the order the block loop below it does (note its `List.rev`s: SILGen builds both
lists newest first). §2 says why they all go here. `irgen-allocas.t` reads `--emit-llvm-allocas`,
which drops every other instruction and every terminator, so it tests this hole alone.

**3. `gen_instr`.** The literal cases, `alloc_stack` and `binop` are already written, as the
pattern to copy. What is left is six instructions, and for each the question is the same: does it
**emit a line**, and does it **produce a result** that later instructions will name?

| instruction | emits a line | binds a result | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `load` | yes | yes | |
| `store` | yes | no | |
| `unop` | yes | yes | `-x` on an `Int` or a `Double` (§2) |
| `function_ref` | **no** | yes | just an operand: `@name` |
| `apply` | yes | only if non-`Void` | `%tK = call …` versus `call void …` |
| `print` | — | — | call `gen_print` |

When an instruction binds a result, give it `fresh_temp ()` and record it with `bind_operand`, so
the instructions after it can `lookup_operand` it. The LLVM text for each line is in §2's table.
A function cannot be valid LLVM without its terminators, so `irgen-instrs.t` reads
`--emit-llvm-instrs`, which prints the instructions and leaves the terminators out. Keep the final
catch-all `failwith` below your cases until you have all six — the file has to compile for any
test to run.

**4. `gen_term`**: four terminators — `br`, `cond_br`, `return` (with or without a value) and
`unreachable`. One special case: `@main` returns `i32` to the operating system, so a `return` with
no value in `main` is `ret i32 0`; `is_main` is in scope for it. Then every test can run whole
programs:

```bash
printf 'var i = 0\nwhile i < 3 {\n  print(i)\n  i = i + 1\n}\n' > p.swift
_build/default/phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm/tests/lab.exe build p.swift -o p && ./p
```

If the IR is not well-typed, clang says so at once, naming the line.

Reference: `solution/irgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm        # add T=irgen-binop to run one file
```

Eight cram files, two unit suites and the oracle. The first four read the IR, one hole each, in
the order of §3; the rest **build the program and run it**, which is the point of this concept:

| file | flag | green with | what it pins |
|---|---|---|---|
| `irgen-binop.t` | `--binop-table` | `binop_instruction` | every operator at `Int`, `Double` and `Bool`: signed `sdiv`/`srem`/`icmp`, the `f` family, ordered `fcmp` and `une` for `!=` |
| `irgen-allocas.t` | `--emit-llvm-allocas` | `gen_allocas` | a loop's `let` hoisted into `bb0`, one typed `alloca` per slot, both arms of an `if`, each function's slots in its own entry |
| `irgen-instrs.t` | `--emit-llvm-instrs` | `gen_instr` | literals as operands, the `alloca`/`load`/`store` model, a `binop` line with its zero guard, `sub i64 0, x` and `fneg` for minus, `function_ref` + `apply` as one `call`, `print`'s two shapes |
| `irgen-terms.t` | `--emit-llvm-terms` | `gen_term` | the four terminators one by one, `@main`'s `ret i32 0`, an `unreachable` that survives into LLVM, and one `build`: printable is not the same as well-typed |
| `run-arith.t` | `build` | all | truncating division and signed remainder, minus, Double comparisons including NaN, `Bool` printing, `&&`/`||` short-circuiting |
| `run-control.t` | `build` | all | `if`/`else if`, `while`, `for` including an empty range, `break`, `continue` in a `for`, nested loops, a `let` in a loop run three million times |
| `run-funcs.t` | `build` | all | argument order and mixed types, nested calls, recursion, mutual recursion, `Void` and an early `return`, `gcd`/`collatz` |
| `oracle.t` | `build` | all | **Milestone M2**: 30 programs built by `swiftc -Onone` and by you, both run, stdout and exit code identical |

Two suites run in-process: `test_irgen.ml` (`irgen`) reads the emitted text to ask *where* a line
landed, which a cram `grep` cannot, with one group per hole;
`test_exercises.ml` (`exercises-09`) holds the three optional §6 exercises.

### Three things worth knowing before you read a red report

**Each hole goes green on its own, in order.** `--binop-table` calls `binop_instruction` with no
program at all. Every other file compiles a program, and every function starts with
`gen_allocas`, so those read `TODO` until it is written. After it, the lab modes stop before what
is not written yet: `--emit-llvm-allocas` drops everything but the slots, and
`--emit-llvm-instrs` leaves the terminators out. Only the `build` files need all four holes.

**The terminator tests are split by kind.** `--emit-llvm-terms <kind>` prints one kind — `br`,
`cond-br`, `return-value`, `return-none` or `unreachable` — so an unfinished one cannot hide a
finished one.

**A program that never ends fails; it does not hang.** Every executable the tests build runs under
a five-second deadline, so a wrong back-edge shows up as exit `124` instead of freezing `make lab`.

## 5. Benchmark it

The benchmark runs this Collatz workload for every starting value below 500,000:

```swift
var total = 0
for start in 1 ..< 500000 {
  var n = start
  while n != 1 {
    if n % 2 == 0 {
      n = n / 2
    } else {
      n = 3 * n + 1
    }
    total = total + 1
  }
}
print(total)
```

Run it from `course/` after completing all four holes:

```console
$ make bench C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm
IRGen runtime benchmark -- Collatz for starts 1..<500000
  output: 62134644 (all five binaries agree)
  native runtime, best of 5 after one warm-up:
    swiftml (clang default)  0.209 s
    swiftml + clang -O2      0.045 s
    swiftc -Onone            0.670 s
    swiftc -O                0.070 s
    swiftc -Ounchecked       0.046 s
  clang -O2 speedup: 4.69x
  swiftc -O speedup: 9.61x
  unchecked gap: 1.02x (swiftc / swiftml)
```

These are measured reference-solution results; timings vary by machine. The runner first requires
byte-identical output from all five binaries, then reports the best of five executions after one
warm-up. It has no speed gate because this concept deliberately emits unoptimized code.

The flags select the optimization level. With no flag, clang uses `-O0`: it preserves the raw
`alloca`, `load`, and `store` heavy shape closely. `clang -O2` enables LLVM's standard optimizations
for speed. `swiftc -Onone` compiles without optimization, while `swiftc -O` compiles with
optimizations for speed. `swiftc -Ounchecked` also optimizes, but removes runtime safety checks such
as integer-overflow checks.

The `clang -O2` row is useful: without changing our SIL, LLVM removes much of the raw memory traffic
and makes the program about 4.65 times faster. For this small scalar subset, we could defer much of
the optimization work to LLVM. That shows IRGen already produces optimization-friendly LLVM IR.

It does not make a SIL optimizer redundant. Swift-specific passes can reason about ownership,
dynamic dispatch, and generics before those ideas disappear into lower-level IR. Optimized SIL can
also feed a backend that does not use LLVM. Phase 4 builds that target-independent layer, starting
with **mem2reg**, then constant folding, CSE, and inlining.

The `-Ounchecked` result makes the comparison clearer. Once swiftc removes its safety checks, its
`0.046 s` is effectively the same as our `0.045 s`. For this non-overflowing scalar workload, both
pipelines therefore hand LLVM code it can optimize to the same performance class.

That result does not establish general performance parity. `-Ounchecked` changes Swift's safety
semantics, and our subset omits most of Swift's language and runtime. The benchmark isolates one
small program and one major source of overhead.

With richer Swift constructs, SIL optimization can produce faster code than a basic translation
straight to LLVM. Reference counting, protocol and class dispatch, generic calls, closure captures,
and `Array` checks still have explicit Swift meaning in SIL. SIL passes can remove redundant
retain/release operations, replace dynamic dispatch with direct calls, specialize generic code, and
eliminate or move collection checks out of loops. A basic lowering turns many of these operations
into pointer loads, stores, and opaque runtime calls; LLVM can no longer recover all the Swift
semantics needed to prove the same transformations. LLVM then optimizes the lower-level result, so
the SIL and LLVM optimizers complement each other. This division is described in
`swift/docs/OptimizerDesign.md` and `swift/docs/HighLevelSILOptimizations.rst`.

## 6. Exercises

These are optional. `make exercises C=phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm` runs only their
self-detecting suite. They also appear in `make lab` as `TODO (optional)` until you start one.

1. **Definite initialization.** Add uninitialized `var x: Int` (a `var` with a type annotation and no
   initializer): parser, an `Ast` node, sema binds it, SILGen `alloc_stack`s but does not `store`.
   Then write a **forward dataflow pass on the SIL CFG**: a slot is "initialized on entry to a block"
   iff it's initialized on exit of *all* predecessors; a `load` from an uninitialized slot is
   "variable '…' used before being initialized." Match `swiftc`.
2. **`Double` output parity.** Print just enough decimal digits to preserve the exact `Double`
   value when the text is parsed again, and make `print(0.1 + 0.2)` match `swiftc`. The problem
   and the algorithms are below.
3. **A tiny runtime.** Add a `runtime.c` (compiled and linked by the driver) with `swiftml_print_int`
   etc., instead of inlining `printf` calls — the seed of a real standard library (Phase 7). How to
   build and run it is below.

**Exercise 2 — what "just enough digits" means.** `0.1 + 0.2` is not 0.3: neither `0.1` nor `0.2`
has an exact binary form, and the `Double` nearest their sum is 0.3000000000000000444…. Every
`Double` is surrounded by a small interval of real numbers that round to it, and any decimal
inside that interval reads back as the same `Double`. Swift prints the one with the *fewest
significant digits*, and the closest to the exact value among those. Fixed precision gets it
wrong both ways:

| C format | `0.1 + 0.2` | `0.1` | Swift prints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%g` (6 digits) | `0.3` — a different `Double` | `0.1` | `0.30000000000000004`, `0.1` |
| `%.17g` (always enough) | `0.30000000000000004` | `0.10000000000000001` — too long | |

The simple correct method: for *n* = 1, 2, … 17, print with *n* significant digits (`%.*e`) and
parse it back with `strtod`; stop at the first *n* that returns the same `Double` (17 always
does). It is exact, and slow only by the standard of a formatter that runs in 10 ns. The fast
algorithms find the shortest digits directly, from the value's binary form `s × 2^e`, with no
trial parsing:

- **Dragon4** (Steele & White, 1990) — the first correct one; exact, using arbitrary-precision
  integers. Ryan Juckett's *Printing Floating-Point Numbers*, a four-part series, builds it up
  from the bit layout: `https://www.ryanjuckett.com/printing-floating-point-numbers/`.
- **Grisu** (Loitsch, 2010) — the same search with 64-bit integers only. Much faster, but for
  about 0.5% of values it cannot prove its answer is shortest and must fall back to a slow path.
  Paper: "Printing Floating-Point Numbers Quickly and Accurately with Integers",
  `https://doi.org/10.1145/1806596.1806623`.
- **Ryū** (Adams, 2018) — always exact with 64/128-bit integers, using a precomputed table of
  powers of 10; no fallback. Paper: `https://doi.org/10.1145/3192366.3192369`; readable C
  reference implementation: `https://github.com/ulfjack/ryu`.

swiftc's own printer, `swift/stdlib/public/core/FloatingPointToString.swift`, draws on Grisu and
on Giulietti's *Schubfach* (2021), a relative of Ryū; its header comment is a good summary. Any of
these methods gives the same digits, so the trial-and-`strtod` loop is a fine answer here. Then
format them the way Swift does: plain notation between 1e-4 and 1e16, with `.0` added to a whole
number (`1.0`, `100.0`), and exponential notation outside it with at least two exponent digits
(`1e-05`, `1e+16`).

**Exercise 3 — building with a runtime.** IRGen stops emitting `printf` and instead declares and
calls your functions:

```llvm
declare void @swiftml_print_int(i64)
...
  call void @swiftml_print_int(i64 %t2)
```

That `.ll` no longer links on its own: the functions live in `runtime.c`, and clang compiles
both and links them into one executable. You can do it by hand before touching the driver:

```bash
L=_build/default/phase2-types-flow/09-sil-to-llvm/tests/lab.exe
$L --emit-llvm p.swift > p.ll                       # calls @swiftml_print_int
clang -c runtime.c -o runtime.o                     # your runtime, compiled once
clang -Wno-override-module p.ll runtime.o -o p && ./p
```

Then make `run_clang` in `driver.ml` do the same: pass `runtime.c` to its clang command beside the
`.ll`. The driver has to find that file wherever `build` is run from (the cram tests run in a
sandbox directory), so either locate it relative to the compiler or carry its text inside the
driver as a string and write it to a temporary file before calling clang.

## 7. Recap & what's next — **Milestone M2**

Phase 2 is complete. In 05–07, you extended every front-end layer — the lexer, parser, AST, and Sema
— to support types, control flow, and functions. This included bidirectional type checking and the
semantic rules that make those constructs sound — and, just as importantly, the discipline that the
checker **produces a typed tree** rather than a verdict, so that every stage after it consumes
decisions instead of re-deriving them. SILGen then added the **SIL** middle (08), and
**IRGen** now lowers SIL to LLVM and runs the result (09). The core pipeline follows swiftc's:
`Parse → Sema → SILGen → SIL → IRGen → LLVM → native`. On the
`Int`/`Bool`/control-flow/functions corpus, the output matches `swiftc` byte-for-byte (`Double`
printing and `String` are the documented gaps of §2).

Two directions open up. **Phase 3** grows the *language* — `struct`, `enum` (ADTs), pattern matching,
`Optional` — the value types Swift is built from. **Phase 4** grows the *compiler* — the SIL
**optimizer**, starting with **mem2reg**, where the raw, load/store-heavy SIL you've been emitting is
promoted to **SSA** and you learn SSA properly, by watching it happen. That's the deliberate payoff of
choosing memory-based SIL back in concept 08.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

Mirrors `solution/irgen.ml`. The shape: a constant maps a SIL value to an LLVM operand; an instruction
emits a line and maps its result to a fresh `%tK`; types come from the function's `val_ty`.

```ocaml
let gen_instr (value, instruction) =
  match (instruction : Sil.instr) with
  | Sil.Int_lit integer -> bind_operand value (string_of_int integer)
  | Sil.Bool_lit boolean -> bind_operand value (if boolean then "1" else "0")
  | Sil.Float_lit number ->
      bind_operand value (Printf.sprintf "0x%016LX" (Int64.bits_of_float number))
  | Sil.String_lit text -> bind_operand value (add_string_const text)
  (* emitted in the entry block by gen_allocas, below — see §2 *)
  | Sil.Alloc_stack _ -> ()
  | Sil.Load address ->
      let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = load %s, ptr %s\n" result_operand
              (llvm_type (value_type value)) (lookup_operand address));
      bind_operand value result_operand
  | Sil.Store (stored_value, address) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  store %s %s, ptr %s\n"
              (llvm_type (value_type stored_value)) (lookup_operand stored_value)
              (lookup_operand address))
  | Sil.Binop (operator, left, right) -> gen_binop value operator left right
  | Sil.Unop (Ast.Neg, operand) ->
      let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
      (if value_type operand = Types.TDouble then
         emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = fneg double %s\n" result_operand (lookup_operand operand))
       else emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = sub i64 0, %s\n" result_operand (lookup_operand operand)));
      bind_operand value result_operand
  | Sil.Func_ref name -> bind_operand value ("@" ^ name)
  | Sil.Apply (function_operand, arguments) ->
      let argument_list =
        String.concat ", "
          (List.map (fun argument ->
             Printf.sprintf "%s %s" (llvm_type (value_type argument))
               (lookup_operand argument)) arguments)
      in
      let return_type = value_type value in
      if return_type = Types.TVoid then
        emit (Printf.sprintf "  call void %s(%s)\n"
                (lookup_operand function_operand) argument_list)
      else (
        let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
        emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = call %s %s(%s)\n" result_operand
                (llvm_type return_type) (lookup_operand function_operand) argument_list);
        bind_operand value result_operand)
  | Sil.Print printed_value -> gen_print printed_value

let gen_term (terminator : Sil.term) =
  match terminator with
  | Sil.Br target -> emit (Printf.sprintf "  br label %%bb%d\n" target)
  | Sil.Cond_br (condition, then_block, else_block) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  br i1 %s, label %%bb%d, label %%bb%d\n"
              (lookup_operand condition) then_block else_block)
  | Sil.Return None -> emit (if is_main then "  ret i32 0\n" else "  ret void\n")
  | Sil.Return (Some return_value) ->
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  ret %s %s\n"
              (llvm_type function_definition.Sil.ret) (lookup_operand return_value))
  | Sil.Unreachable -> emit "  unreachable\n"

let gen_allocas () =
  List.iter
    (fun (block : Sil.block) ->
      List.iter
        (fun (value, instruction) ->
          match (instruction : Sil.instr) with
          | Sil.Alloc_stack _ ->
              let stack_operand = fresh_temp () in
              emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = alloca %s\n" stack_operand
                      (llvm_type (value_type value)));
              bind_operand value stack_operand
          | _ -> ())
        (List.rev block.Sil.instrs))
    (List.rev function_definition.Sil.blocks)
```

And the table, `binop_instruction`:

```ocaml
let binop_instruction (operator : Ast.binop) (operand_type : Types.ty) : string =
  match (operator, operand_type) with
  | Ast.Add, Types.TInt -> "add i64"
  | Ast.Sub, Types.TInt -> "sub i64"
  | Ast.Mul, Types.TInt -> "mul i64"
  | Ast.Div, Types.TInt -> "sdiv i64"
  | Ast.Mod, Types.TInt -> "srem i64"
  | Ast.Add, Types.TDouble -> "fadd double"
  | Ast.Sub, Types.TDouble -> "fsub double"
  | Ast.Mul, Types.TDouble -> "fmul double"
  | Ast.Div, Types.TDouble -> "fdiv double"
  | Ast.Eq, Types.TInt -> "icmp eq i64"
  | Ast.Ne, Types.TInt -> "icmp ne i64"
  | Ast.Lt, Types.TInt -> "icmp slt i64"
  | Ast.Le, Types.TInt -> "icmp sle i64"
  | Ast.Gt, Types.TInt -> "icmp sgt i64"
  | Ast.Ge, Types.TInt -> "icmp sge i64"
  | Ast.Eq, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp oeq double"
  | Ast.Ne, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp une double"
  | Ast.Lt, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp olt double"
  | Ast.Le, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp ole double"
  | Ast.Gt, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp ogt double"
  | Ast.Ge, Types.TDouble -> "fcmp oge double"
  | Ast.Eq, Types.TBool -> "icmp eq i1"
  | Ast.Ne, Types.TBool -> "icmp ne i1"
  (* nothing else arrives: SILGen lowered && and || to branches, and the String
     operators are not lowered in this subset *)
  | _ -> failwith "IRGen: no LLVM instruction for this binop"
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — definite initialization (a SIL dataflow pass)

With `var x: Int` lowering to an `alloc_stack` and no `store`, run a forward dataflow over the SIL
CFG. For each block compute `in[b] = ⋂ out[p]` over predecessors `p` (the entry's `in` is the empty
set; a parameter slot starts initialized); walk the block updating the set on each `Store`, and on a
`Load` of a slot **not** in the set, report "variable '…' used before being initialized." Iterate to a
fixed point (a worklist). This is the same forward-meet-over-paths shape you'll reuse for liveness
and reaching-definitions in Phase 4 — definite initialization is the gentlest instance, and it's
*mandatory* in swiftc because it's a soundness guarantee, not an optimization.

### 2 — Double output parity

The key (`solution/exercises/driver.ml`, `swiftml_print_double` in the runtime it carries) uses
the trial loop from §6: for `p` = 1 … 17, `snprintf(buf, …, "%.*e", p - 1, d)` and keep the first
`buf` that `strtod` turns back into `d`. That string is `[-]D.DDDe±XX`, so the rest is splitting
it into sign, digits and decimal exponent, dropping trailing zeros, and laying the digits out in
Swift's form: exponential when the exponent is below -4 or at least 16, otherwise plain, padding
with zeros and adding `.0` to a whole number. NaN and the infinities print as `nan`, `inf`,
`-inf`. Checked against `swiftc`, including `0.1`, `1.0`, `100.0`, `0.30000000000000004`,
`0.3333333333333333`, `1e+16`, `1e-05`, `0.0001` and the three special values.

### 3 — a runtime.c

Have the driver also compile a small `runtime.c` (declaring `void swiftml_print_int(long long)` etc.)
and link it in, and make IRGen `call @swiftml_print_int` instead of inlining `printf`. Now the
print/format logic lives in C you control — the first brick of a standard library, which Phase 7
turns into `Array`/`String`/`Dictionary`.
```
